Four Touching Circles 3

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Four circles touch their neighbours in a ring, and you can move them to see when their four touching spots lie on one circle.
How to play: Drag a circle's centre dot or its rim dot, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the dots, centre lines, circles or inverted picture, and press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

Four circles can be arranged in a ring so that each touches its two neighbours. Mark the four places where they touch. Sometimes the marks sit on one circle and sometimes they do not. What decides it?

Outside touches and inside touches

Two tangent circles can touch in two ways. In an outside touch the centres are r1 + r2 apart. In an inside touch one circle surrounds the other and the centres are |r1 − r2| apart. The ring has four touches, so the number of outside touches is even (0, 2 or 4) or odd (1 or 3). The third applet lets you drag circles into either case; the first applet's inversion kept only the even ones, which is why its original claim was too broad.

Why parity decides it

Give each circle a signed radius. For an outside touch give the two circles the same sign, so their centre distance is |s1 + s2|. For an inside touch give them opposite signs. Going round a closed ring, such a choice of signs is possible exactly when the number of inside touches is even — the same as saying the number of outside touches is even. This is the parity at the heart of the claim.

With consistent signs, invert the picture at one contact point. The two circles meeting there become parallel lines; the other two become tangent circles, each touching one of the lines. Those two images are homothetic about their own contact point, so the three other contact points line up. Undoing the inversion turns that line into a circle through the contact point you chose. When parity is odd, no consistent signing exists and the fourth mark really is off the circle.

What the test found

The page's exact claim is: the four contact points lie on a circle if the number of outside touches is even, and not otherwise. The logic test built closed rings for all 16 outside/inside patterns with eight sets of radii and hundreds of closing angles, and checked both the concyclicity determinant and the applet's own circle through the first three contacts. The claim held for every ring tested — odd rings left the fourth point clearly off the dashed circle.

A few harmless applet details stay: it accepts a touch within 2 pixels (3 once three marks exist), it builds its circle from the first three marks with GetCircle, and its ShowTangents field and SetEnabled method are leftovers with no working checkbox. Its opening circles were random; here they start as a fixed ring with four outside touches so the claim is visible at once. Only the presentation changed: SVG handles and site colours instead of AWT panels.

Tick Inversion and drag the grey circle's centre onto a yellow contact point: the two circles touching there turn into two parallel lines.
